conversation_lines.text: Mainly watch for dizziness or weakness—signs of low blood pressure or electrolyte imbalance. We’ll check your labs regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we removed your infected tunneled line. The tip was sent for culture to confirm the bacteria. You’re now on a temporary internal jugular line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not really—just until we place a new PICC. We tried a left-sided PICC, but it coiled in the subclavian vein and wasn’t usable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that didn’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, so we used a temporary line in your neck. Tomorrow, we’ll try placing a PICC on the right side using your basilic vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just placed a new double-lumen PICC in your right arm. It’s in the correct position, and you can start using it right away for your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Is the old line infection under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, meropenem is working. We’ll continue for two weeks. Also, your NG tube clogged last night, so we replaced it and advanced it past your stomach under X-ray guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that’s why I felt blocked. Is the new one working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s in the third part of your duodenum and ready for feeds. We’ll keep your tube feeds going at 65 cc/hr.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your arms to check your veins. There’s a small clot in your right basilic vein, but it’s not blocking blood flow, so we don’t need to treat it now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this time. It’s nonocclusive, and your vein is still open. We’ll monitor it. Given your condition, we avoid blood thinners unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another paracentesis yesterday—removed over 5 liters of fluid. Your abdomen should feel less tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can breathe easier now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep doing these weekly since your ascites is diuretic-resistant. Your liver function tests are stable, and your mental status remains clear—no signs of hepatic encephalopathy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed lactulose, so that’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. As long as you’re alert and having regular bowel movements, we’ll continue rifaximin and hold lactulose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest blood cultures are negative—great news. That means the antibiotic is clearing the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m almost done?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the full 14-day course. Then, in two weeks, we’ll repeat cultures. If still negative, you can get a new tunneled line placed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Much improved. We believe it’s due to Remodulin, not infection. Keep using loperamide as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my cipro? I was on it for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it during treatment, but you should restart it once antibiotics are done to prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll finish your meropenem at home via the PICC line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How will I get the antibiotics at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A home health nurse will come twice a day to give the IV dose. When you finish, you’ll get blood cultures. If negative, you can have your tunneled line replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your home medications. Increase spironolactone to 200 mg and torsemide to 60 mg daily. Restart cipro after antibiotics. Use loperamide for diarrhea as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my liver clinic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’ll need labs checked at your next paracentesis. Also, you received your flu shot while here—good protection for this season.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and call if anything changes before your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I’m Dr. ___. You’re here today because you need a right heart catheterization to check your pulmonary pressures as part of your transplant evaluation. We’ll start with some IV diuresis to get your fluid down first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, yes. I’ve been feeling a bit bloated and my breathing’s been a little harder, but not worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows ascites, and your weight is up. We’ll give you IV furosemide to help remove the extra fluid. You’ve been on spironolactone and torsemide at home—we’ll hold those for now while we use the IV version.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And what about my PICC line? I had my old tunneled line removed last time because of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your recent blood cultures were negative, so the infection appears cleared. We’ll place a new tunneled catheter later this week so you can go home with a more permanent line for your Remodulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about staying on the PICC long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll make sure it’s done safely. Also, your diarrhea has improved since last admission, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s back to my baseline—soft stools a few times a day. I haven’t needed Imodium much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. We still think it’s related to the Remodulin. We’ll keep Imodium available if it flares up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver team said I’m still on the transplant list. Is this cath going to affect that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly why we’re doing it. We need to confirm your pulmonary pressures are stable enough for transplant. So far, everything looks favorable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray after admission confirms the PICC is in good position—tip in the lower SVC, no pneumothorax. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I didn’t feel any pain during placement, so that’s a plus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs show low platelets and mild anemia, which we expect with cirrhosis. Liver enzymes are stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any sign of infection? I’m still nervous after the Acinetobacter last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures from yesterday showed no growth. That’s excellent. It means no active bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. That really helps me relax a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to do a paracentesis today. Your belly is still quite full, and removing some fluid will help your breathing and comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll numb the area first. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. We’ll remove about 1.25 liters—enough to help, but not so much that it drops your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We removed 1.25 liters of fluid. The sample shows a few white cells but no bacteria—so no sign of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my ciprofloxacin? I’m still on that for prevention, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing your daily ciprofloxacin to prevent infection. Your peritoneal fluid culture will be final in a few days, but early signs are reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is coming down—now at 98 kg from 103.6. That’s progress. We’ll keep the IV lasix going another day before the heart cath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe a little easier already. My legs aren’t as swollen either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly what we want to see. Your lungs sounded clearer this morning—no crackles at the bases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today we’re placing your new tunneled catheter. It’ll go into your right internal jugular vein and the tip will sit in your right atrium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—fentanyl and versed—so you’ll be relaxed and may not remember much. We’ll monitor your oxygen closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tunneled line was placed successfully. Fluoroscopy confirmed the tip is in the right atrium. Your PICC will be removed tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel more secure with a tunneled line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show stable liver function. Albumin is 3.4, which is good. Creatinine is up a bit to 0.9, but still in normal range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re watching it closely. We’ll reduce the IV lasix today and prepare for your heart cath tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow is your right heart catheterization. It’s a short procedure—about an hour. You’ll be awake but sedated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any risks I should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very low risk. We’ll monitor your pressures in real time. The main goal is to confirm your pulmonary artery pressure is low enough for transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your right heart cath is complete. Pressures are borderline normal. Mean PA pressure is 24, which is slightly improved from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean I’m still a transplant candidate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—no contraindication. Your cardiac output is a bit high, which is common in cirrhosis, but everything else looks good. You can continue on Remodulin and sildenafil.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a huge relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Probably tomorrow. We’ll finish your IV diuresis today. Your weight is now 92 kg—close to your dry weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. Your tunneled line is in place, PICC is out, and you’ve completed your diuresis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Restart your home spironolactone and torsemide tomorrow. If your weight goes up more than three pounds, call the liver team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue at 65 ml/hour. You’re on Jevity 1.5—same as before. Keep the low-sodium diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a paracentesis scheduled soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. The liver team will follow up and order labs when you come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? I’ve been using Dilaudid for my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue MS Contin 60 mg every 8 hours and Dilaudid as needed. You’ve had compression fractures, so we’ll keep that regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And testosterone patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the 4 mg patch daily. No changes there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You look better too—clear mental status, no asterixis, breathing well. Your encephalopathy is stable. Keep taking rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And nadolol for my varices?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue 20 mg daily. Last EGD showed grade II varices, so it’s important for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Keep monitoring your weight, take your meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your discharge instructions say to restart torsemide and spironolactone tomorrow. Don’t start today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your ciprofloxacin—keep taking it daily. It helps prevent infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. The nurse will go over your prescriptions and wound care for the tunneled line site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is a little dried blood under the dressing normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, some dried blood is expected. Just watch for redness, swelling, or pus—those would be signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And continue your Remodulin through the new line. The home team will coordinate the pump setup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already confirmed with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re all set for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will bring the wheelchair shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your MELD score was 31 before admission. That keeps you high on the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Fingers crossed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re rooting for you. Stay in touch with the liver team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I understand you've been feeling unwell. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve had a headache, stomachache, and no appetite for a couple days. I had a low fever yesterday—around 100.3. I get those sometimes with infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chills, cough, or sore throat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No chills or cough. But I do feel short of breath and my sinuses are congested. My belly feels more swollen than usual too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned you were with your niece who was sick—any chance you caught something from her?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She had cold symptoms, so maybe. But I’m worried—my tunneled line has caused infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check that carefully. We’re going to run blood tests, a urine test, and possibly a paracentesis to make sure there’s no infection in your ascites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just feel so tired and achy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on you. Your vitals are stable—temperature is normal now, heart rate and oxygen levels are okay on your usual 4 liters of oxygen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood and urine cultures came back with no growth so far. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. So it’s not a blood infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not from what we see so far. But we’ll keep monitoring. We’re also going to do a CT scan to check your liver and lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Your liver looks stable with cirrhosis and varices, but we see a couple of new small spots—one in the liver and one in the lung. Nothing looks like an abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they cancerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Too early to say. They could be benign. We’ll follow up with your liver team. Nothing urgent, but we’ll keep an eye on them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat blood cultures are negative. No sign of bacteremia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But I still feel awful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. Your chest X-ray shows some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—but no pneumonia. We think you have a viral upper respiratory infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just a cold?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely, yes. We’ll treat your symptoms. We’re also going to do a paracentesis today to check your ascites fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just removed 2 liters of fluid from your abdomen. It was reddish, but that’s not uncommon. We’ll test it to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help? My belly still feels full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help over the next few hours. We’ll keep monitoring your comfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fluid analysis shows a white blood cell count slightly elevated but no bacteria seen. Culture is negative. So no sign of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not an infection in the belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. We think your symptoms are from the viral URI. We’ll give you a nasal spray—fluticasone—to help with congestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep Ativan available for nausea. It should improve as you start feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Still tired, but the congestion is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your CMV and EBV tests came back negative. No other viruses detected. We’re confident it’s a mild viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver and transplant status?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MELD labs are stable. You’re still on the transplant list. The portopulmonary hypertension is stable on your current meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re looking better. Your breathing is easier, and your exam shows less abdominal tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. But I’ve been gaining weight—worried it’s more fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nutrition saw you. They think you might be getting too many calories from the tube feeds. They recommend reducing from 18 to 16 hours a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So cut back on the feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, same rate, just shorter time. We’ll monitor your weight daily. Call if it goes up more than 3 pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat blood cultures are negative. You’re improving steadily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed pain meds much. And no nausea since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow if you keep this up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. We’ll discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about the nasal spray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with fluticasone—use it twice daily for congestion. Continue all your regular meds, including rifaximin, nadolol, and Remodulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Reduce to 16 hours a day. Follow up with the liver clinic as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spots on the CT?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver and kidney findings need follow-up imaging. Your liver team will arrange that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad it wasn’t another serious infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you dodged that. Keep using the nasal spray, watch your weight, and call if you develop fever or worsening symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, we’ve admitted you today because you’re getting your liver transplant. You’ve been on the list for a while, and a donor has become available.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doc. I’m ready. I’ve been waiting for this. How soon will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The surgery is scheduled for this morning. We’ll take you to the OR around noon. You’ll be under general anesthesia, and the team will replace your liver with the donor’s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pulmonary hypertension? I’m still on Remodulin. Will that be okay during surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your Remodulin running throughout. We’ll also use nitric oxide during the surgery to help keep your pulmonary pressures low and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m nervous, but I trust you. What about recovery after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go to the ICU after. We’ll monitor your new liver closely—check blood flow, liver enzymes, and how you’re tolerating the transplant. You’ll be on a ventilator at first, but we hope to take you off soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just updating you—we’ve completed the liver transplant. It went smoothly. The new liver is in, and blood flow looks good so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your liver this evening. The hepatic artery and portal vein are both open and flowing well. There’s some expected swelling, but nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My breathing feels a bit heavy though. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re still on the ventilator, and we see some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—on the X-ray. We’re suctioning and adjusting your settings to help expand your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your liver enzymes are starting to come down. That’s a sign the new liver is functioning. We’re also seeing improvement in your chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. When can I breathe on my own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try to wean you off the ventilator tomorrow. Your pressures are stable, and we’ve started sildenafil to help with your pulmonary hypertension instead of nitric oxide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re off the nitric oxide, and your PA pressures are still under 40. That’s excellent. We’ll keep you on sildenafil three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better already. Any sign of rejection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’re monitoring your tacrolimus levels daily and adjusting your immunosuppressants. So far, no signs of rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been extubated and are breathing on your own. Swan-Ganz catheter has been removed. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. Can I sit up now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll start physical therapy soon. Your drain output is high, so we’re giving albumin to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a new central line today to help with medications and monitoring. Your kidney function is a bit off—we’re watching it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the surgery or my old kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a mix. We’ve reduced Valcyte because it can affect kidneys. We expect it to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are trending well—creatinine is down, liver enzymes continue to improve. You’re moving to the regular floor today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel stronger. Any more tests coming up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep doing daily labs. The team is happy with your progress so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still stable. Your Remodulin dose was slightly reduced to 42 ng/kg/min. You’re tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any reason for the change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pulmonary pressures are stable, so we’re cautiously reducing it. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urine culture shows minimal growth—nothing to treat. You remain afebrile and stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another liver ultrasound this morning. We’re seeing gas in the liver—especially the left lobe—and some signs of possible infarction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gas? In my liver? That sounds bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is concerning. It could mean an infection or poor blood flow. We’re ordering a CT scan to get a better look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows multiple infarcts in the left lobe and some in the right. There’s air in the liver, which suggests a gas-forming infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Infection? But I haven’t had a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Immunosuppressants can mask symptoms. We’ve started broad-spectrum antibiotics and are preparing for surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate and breathing are increasing. We’re moving you to the ICU.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve intubated you because your oxygen levels dropped. We’re giving pressors to support your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood cultures are back. They show E. coli. It’s likely the infection came from the donor liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the transplant… it’s infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It appears so. We’re taking you to surgery to remove the infected tissue and check the blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Post-op update: we found a large abscess with gas. We couldn’t drain it fully, but we removed necrotic tissue and checked the hepatic artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the liver still working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, the damage is severe. Your liver enzymes are very high, and your kidneys are failing. We’ve started CVVH.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with your health care proxy. Given how sick you are, we’re shifting to comfort care only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So… no more fighting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you comfortable. You’re not alone. We’re here with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure is dropping despite four pressors. Your organs are shutting down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m tired… just let me go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re with you. You’re safe. We’ll keep you pain-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, I’m sorry. Despite everything, your body couldn’t recover. You passed peacefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe the E. coli came from the donor, who had a history of IV drug use. It seeded the liver before transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll inform your family and begin the process of notifying the transplant network about the donor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The cultures from the liver tissue confirmed E. coli, matching the blood results. It was a multi-drug resistant strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re documenting everything for the medical review board. This was an unexpected complication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your care team is grieving with your family. You were a strong patient, and we did everything we could.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring for any public health implications due to the resistant E. coli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The hospital chaplain has spoken with your proxy. They’re arranging next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve completed the post-mortem documentation. Your case will be reviewed to improve future transplant safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. ___, thank you for your courage. You faced this with dignity. We’ll remember you.
